The U.S. economy grew faster over the summer than it did during the spring, but prices are also rising fast, NPR's Steve Bissaha reports.
Gross domestic product for the U.S. grew at an annual rate of 3.4 percent, according to a new report out today from the Commerce Department.
That's for July, August, and September, and faster than the 2.2 percent growth from the spring.
One reason for the growth is the major investment in artificial intelligence by tech companies.
All the construction and jobs needed to build data centers boosted the economy.
But the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation released today showed prices in September were 3.6 percent higher than a year ago.
Those prices are top of mind for voters as they head to the polls for the midterm elections next week.
Stephen Bissaha, NPR News. Sir Patrick Stewart has died. A spokesperson said he died from a "brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia."
He was 86. Adya Jima-Brompong has this remembrance.
Patrick Stewart spent his career charting the future. He played mutant leader Charles Xavier in The X-Men and Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek The Next Generation.
And to make sure history never forgets the name, enterprise.
Stewart was trained as a Shakespearean actor. He brought that gravitas to all of his roles, along with a playful sense of purpose.
He was also a domestic violence prevention advocate. Sir Patrick Stewart was knighted in 2010 for services to drama.
For NPR News, I'm Adjua Jima-Brompong. This winter's forecast is out. National weather agencies say a super El Nino is changing weather patterns across the globe.
And Pierre's Eva Berger reports. We are in for a warmer and wetter winter. You can think El Nino. It's a natural climate pattern that happens every few years.
Josh Willis is a climate scientist at NASA. It rises up out of the ocean like Godzilla and it breathes fire on Indonesia and Southeast Asia.

Nor'easters tend to have a higher chance of walloping the East Coast. The West Coast already has higher sea levels.
NPR's Eva Berger reporting. It's NPR. A South Korean special prosecutor is calling for the death penalty for ousted President Yoon Seok-yul.
It comes ahead of an appeals court verdict on rebellion charges related to when he briefly declared martial law in December 2024.
Yoon is appealing a life sentence for illegally mobilizing troops to seize the legislature. Prosecutors argue his actions threaten democracy.
South Korea has not executed anyone since 1997. Yoon's legal team claims the martial law was to raise awareness, not establish authoritarian rule.
The head of California's High Speed Rail Authority has resigned. NPR's Joel Rose reports his abrupt departure raises more questions about the future of the troubled project.
Embattled CEO Ian Choudry resigned late Wednesday, according to the chair of the board overseeing the California High Speed Rail Authority.
Choudry led the agency through two tumultuous years. Last month, the Rail Authority's inspector general found the agency had spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on questionable travel expenses.
The ambitious mega project is decades behind schedule and billions of dollars over budget, while its proposed route has been scaled back.
Last year, the Trump administration canceled billions of dollars in federal funds for what it calls a "train to nowhere."
The Rail Authority's board disputes that framing and says the project will move forward under an interim CEO. Joel Rose, NPR News.
